extracted.intended_audience: public health communicators, journalists, and information managers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on identifying, monitoring, and responding to health-related misinformation and disinformation during outbreaks, including verification practices, communication strategies, and cross-sector engagement. Emphasizes newsroom and public-health-oriented tactics for detection, debunking and message design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish misinformation from disinformation
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiate inadvertent sharing of false information (misinformation) from deliberate creation and sharing of information known to be false (disinformation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these distinct definitions to shape responses and choose interventions (e.g., education for misinformation vs. countermeasures and exposure for disinformation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify user-generated content and eyewitness reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Vetting user-generated social media content and eyewitness material is essential before reporting or amplifying it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Train journalists in verification best practice: identify original sources, confirm provenance, and avoid publishing unverified eyewitness posts. Wardle's early BBC work emphasizes newsroom implementation of verification methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use collaborative journalism (Crosscheck) to validate content
rubrics_metrics.description: Bring competing newsrooms together to cross-check stories and co-publish validated content to boost trust and verification capacity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Crosscheck (France, 2017) united 37 newsrooms to jointly identify and report false, misleading, and confusing content; validated items displayed logos side-by-side to increase audience trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain human oversight in automated monitoring
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ AI/ML tools to speed monitoring but retain humans for interpretation and nuanced judgement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AI is useful for graphic content and large-scale pattern detection, but struggles with satire, irony and reframed true content; disinformation often contains a 'kernel of truth' designed to fool algorithms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operate a dedicated health-and-science monitoring team
rubrics_metrics.description: Have a specialized team focused on health narratives, leveraging lessons from political misinformation monitoring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The team should follow targeted accounts, watch for hashtag changes used to evade bans, and examine narratives to surface false or misleading stories for exposure and debunking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitor hashtags and evasive tactics
rubrics_metrics.description: Track shifts in hashtags and other platform tactics used to evade moderation or bans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor hashtag changes and evasive language patterns so that moderation and alerts remain effective even when actors attempt to circumvent rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use content discovery and analytics tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Deploy analytics and discovery tools to report on what’s happening across social media and how content is being shared.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine tool outputs with human analysts to prioritize narratives, detect emerging trends (e.g., #filmyourhospital), and coordinate responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify, expose and debunk false or misleading narratives
rubrics_metrics.description: Actively surface and correct false narratives rather than ignoring them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Produce briefing documents, alerts and debunking pieces (e.g., around hydroxychloroquine or vaccine narratives) and share them with networks of journalists and health professionals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Share timely briefings and daily communications among networks
rubrics_metrics.description: Use an online platform to circulate alerts, briefings and documents to networks of journalists and collaborators frequently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regular, rapid sharing increases situational awareness and enables coordinated exposure/verification efforts across geographies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid public real-time expert debates on unsettled technical details
rubrics_metrics.description: Limit public airing of ongoing expert debates that could create impression of official uncertainty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wardle notes examples (mask messaging, airborne transmission, vaccine dosage) where experts publicly debating on Twitter confused audiences; such technical discussions should be managed so they don't undermine public confidence or be weaponized by bad actors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage and communicate uncertainty carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that rapidly evolving evidence and visible uncertainty can be weaponized; design communications to reduce misinterpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious about overexposing scientific uncertainty in public channels; provide clear core messages and guidance so audiences can find reliable advice during shifting evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communicate complexity using accessible metaphors and emotional connection
rubrics_metrics.description: Translate complex scientific concepts into easy-to-understand messages that also create an emotional connection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use examples like 'flatten the curve' to make abstract concepts tangible and appeal to solidarity with frontline workers; emotionalization helps messages stick but must be used responsibly (misinformation actors also use emotion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid paternalistic, purely science-based broadcast approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: Move beyond one-way, purely technical broadcasts that assume audiences process information like scientists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor messaging to how people filter information through beliefs, biases and emotions; recognize social media as fragmented and mediated by influencers rather than a homogeneous space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engage trusted influencers and diverse channels
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that many people rely on social influencers; partner with them to disseminate authoritative public-health messages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adapt communication strategies to fragmented information ecosystems by leveraging non-traditional trusted sources rather than relying solely on official outlets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build capacity by training public-health professionals in infodemic management
rubrics_metrics.description: Train health professionals, social scientists and journalists together to understand how misinformation impacts information delivery and to improve response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: WHO's infodemic management training webinar (June 2020) brought multiple disciplines together; First Draft began offering training for health professionals in 2020.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engage tech platforms and other stakeholders to amplify authoritative content
rubrics_metrics.description: Work with technology companies and other stakeholders to implement changes that direct attention toward reliable information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include WHO's Facebook Messenger Health Alert, Google's COVID-19 portal, and Twitter strengthening policies to de-prioritize content that conflicts with authoritative public-health guidance. Partnerships are essential given resource constraints of public health communicators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize limited resources and seek collaborative amplification
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledge that public-health communicators often lack resources to compete with misinformation and should therefore partner widely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Engage other stakeholders (newsrooms, tech companies, influencers) to extend reach and leverage alliances to make authoritative messaging more visible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate and understand adversary tactics (reframing, kernel-of-truth)
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware that effective disinformation often uses genuine content reframed or tweaked to produce misleading conclusions and may deliberately exploit truths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use human analysts to detect reframing and contextual manipulation that automated systems may miss; tailor rebuttals to address the kernel of truth rather than only denying claims.
